title: Craters and Seas on the Moon
objective: After this level you can explain where lunar craters and the dark “seas” came from and why they last so long.
summary: Craters are impact scars preserved for billions of years; the dark maria are ancient hardened lava.

cards.headline: The "Man in the Moon" is made of ancient lava.
cards.body: Look at a full Moon and you see a face. Look again and you're reading billions of years of history, written in lava and craters.

cards.headline: Scars that never heal
cards.body: The Moon's craters were blasted out by asteroids and comets, and they range from tiny pits to basins hundreds of kilometers across. What's surprising is how long they last. The Moon has almost no atmosphere, no liquid water and no plate tectonics. Nothing wears its craters away, so they survive for billions of years. Every hit the Moon has taken, from the smallest pit to the biggest basin, is still on the record. The Moon never tidies up.
cards.callout: No air, no water, no erasing

cards.headline: Seas without water
cards.body: The dark patches are called maria, Latin for "seas." They're vast plains of ancient lava that cooled and hardened: seas of rock, named for water that was never there. Most maria sit on the near side, the side that always faces Earth. So the "Man in the Moon" isn't just a face. He's a face that's always turned our way.

cards.headline: Lunar surface: surveyed
learned: Craters come from asteroid and comet impacts
No air, water or plate tectonics erase them
Maria are plains of ancient hardened lava
Most maria are on the near side

questions.prompt: What are the dark patches on the Moon, called maria?

options.label: Oceans of water
options.rationale: The name means “seas,” but they’re dry.

options.label: Shadows of mountains
options.rationale: The patches are dark rock, not shadows.

options.label: Areas the Sun never lights
options.rationale: Sunlight reaches them like the rest of the surface.

questions.explanation: The maria are enormous plains of lava that erupted and hardened long ago.

questions.prompt: Why do craters last so much longer on the Moon than on Earth?

options.label: The Moon is hit by far fewer asteroids than Earth
options.rationale: It’s more that nothing erases the craters.

options.label: It has almost no air, no liquid water and no plate tectonics
Moon rock is much harder than rock on Earth
options.rationale: The difference is what wears craters away.

options.label: The Moon’s stronger gravity holds craters in shape
options.rationale: The Moon’s gravity is weaker than Earth’s.

questions.explanation: With almost no atmosphere, no liquid water and no plate tectonics, nothing wears the Moon’s craters away, so they survive for billions of years.

questions.prompt: From Level 6: why can we see most of the Moon’s maria from Earth?

options.label: The maria reflect more sunlight than the rest of the Moon
options.rationale: They’re actually darker than the rest of the Moon.

options.label: The Moon rotates, so over a month we see every side
options.rationale: The Moon is tidally locked; we see one side.

options.label: The far side is smooth, with no craters or seas
options.rationale: The far side is heavily cratered.

options.label: Most maria are on the near side, which always faces Earth

questions.explanation: The Moon is tidally locked, always showing us the same face, and most of the maria are on that near side.
